balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Computershare Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

marginIncome.title: Margin income
marginIncome.content:
Margin income is interest CPU earns on client cash balances it holds in a fiduciary/custodial capacity as part of registry, corporate trust and employee share plan administration -- not interest on CPU's own cash, and not a lending book.

For Computershare Limited: margin income was $748.7m in FY2026 (~23% of revenue) on average client balances of ~$31.7bn, and carries a disproportionately higher share of profit than its revenue share suggests (near-100% incremental margin). It fell in FY2026 as rates cut but was offset by lower interest expense on CPU's own floating-rate debt -- a natural hedge. Management guides it to recover to ~$770m in FY2027 as balances grow (~$32.8bn) and the hedged share of exposed balances rises from ~50% to ~60%.

What to watch:

  • Central bank rate decisions in the US, UK, Canada and Australia -- CPU does not control this line
  • Average client balances growing (deposit base) versus the yield earned on them
  • The hedged/exposed balance split management discloses each result

clientBalances.title: Average client balances and shareholder accounts
clientBalances.content:
Average client balances is the pool of client cash CPU holds and earns margin income on. Shareholder accounts is the registry record count CPU administers for issuers.

For Computershare Limited: balances (~$31.7bn in FY26) are the base that margin income is earned on; the account count (~33.9m in FY26) is the underlying registry-maintenance volume that recurring fee revenue scales with, independent of the rate cycle.

What to watch:

  • Balances growing from new mandates versus one large client's balance mix shifting (a named risk: Corporate Trust client growth skewed toward non-exposed balances)
  • Account count as a proxy for the sticky, non-rate-sensitive half of the business

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Computershare Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Computershare Limited: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Computershare Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Computershare Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Computershare Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Computershare Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Computershare Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Computershare Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Computershare Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
